headline: The dependency list itself is lean: 51 runtime packages for 473,000 lines, none without an importer, and every heavy browser library (3D viewer, video and AVIF encoders, code editor, Stripe elements) is loaded only on the press that needs it, so a shopper's first scripts carry no third-party library beyond React and Next. The bloat is in when server packages load: the built output shows 89 to 98% of the 830 routes evaluate the same 11 MB of server code on their first request, and with it 481 table definitions nobody queries through, the Stripe and Supabase SDKs, a font parser and sharp's 18 MB native library; the page-view beacon evaluates 1,415 of its 1,456 modules. On the owner's side, supabase-js and zod are 29% of the admin shell's first scripts, and the rich text editor loads on 21 list and detail screens that may never show it. All of it is cheap to fix (mostly under a day each), and two of the items in the existing plan that touch dependencies (FH12) name the wrong package.

clean: No dead dependency: every package in package.json has an importer in src, scripts, e2e or a config file. three and @tiptap/pm have no import of their own but are required peers of @google/model-viewer and tiptap.

Heavy browser libraries are all behind import() at the point of use: @google/model-viewer with three (product-gallery.tsx:349, on the View in 3D press), mediabunny (video-compress.ts:25, :51), @jsquash/avif (image-compress.ts:115, taking the single-threaded encoder directly), the six @codemirror packages (css-panel.tsx:22), all four @stripe browser packages (lazy/shop.tsx:15, express-area.tsx:64, klarna-message.tsx:23, stripe-connect.tsx:8), @supabase/realtime-js (use-support-channel.ts:43), web-vitals (speed-beacon.tsx) and motion (only scroll(), 8.4 KB, only for browsers without CSS scroll timelines).

Shoppers get no third-party runtime library in their first scripts, and that is held by two checks: src/lib/storefront-bundle.scan.test.ts (no zod, page model or full interface text in a visitor's client graph) and e2e/performance.spec.ts (byte budgets, no ZodError in the scripts).

Tree-shaking works where it matters: no unused simple-icons or lucide icon is in any client or server chunk, zod's locales are in no chunk, @vercel/functions brings only attachDatabasePool (its oidc code is not in the health route's chunks), and postgres.js and PGlite are in no server chunk.
lucide-react is imported by name in 24 files (about 168 icons), never as a namespace; the storefront's icon component is a server component.

Server-side single-purpose packages that are already loaded on demand: playwright-core and @sparticuz/chromium (browser.ts:11, :15; traced into 12 routes only), mammoth and unpdf (knowledge.ts:70, :75; bill-reading.ts:54), subset-font, fontverter and HarfBuzz's wasm (one route, the dispatcher), web-push (7 entries). Their features are unused in production today (knowledge_documents, push_subscriptions, product_passports and invoices have never held a row) but they cost nothing per request.

drizzle-orm is used as a `sql` tag plus drizzle-kit's migration differ. Bundled and tree-shaken it is 70 to 90 KB. That is a sound use; replacing it with a hand-written tag would save little and lose the differ. Only the schema's presence at run time is waste (DP-1).
Two Postgres drivers have a recorded reason (client.ts:56-63, D37): pg is the run-time driver; postgres.js serves the build's host read, the migration scripts and tests, and never reaches a function.
pnpm-workspace.yaml: five overrides, each with its advisory and reason; one 7.8 KB patch to Next (D423) with a test that says when to drop it. CI runs pnpm audit --prod (ci.yml:75).

The four @supabase packages do not duplicate each other: @supabase/ssr needs supabase-js as a peer, and realtime-js is the same version supabase-js already brings, listed so the chat can import it alone.

No hand-rolled copy of an installed package was found: Stripe webhook signatures use the SDK's constructEvent, QR codes exist once (lib/qr.ts), the two-step QR comes from the Auth server, and lib/image-size.ts and lib/font-axes.ts read headers by hand precisely to avoid loading sharp and a font library.

findings.title: 481 table definitions are loaded and indexed in every function for a query API nobody calls
findings.evidence: client.ts imports all of schema.ts and passes it to drizzle(), which only enables the relational db.query API. Outside tests there are 0 query-builder or db.query calls and 0 relations(); 5,163 reads and writes go through execute() with the sql tag. In the build the schema module is 600 KB minified, sits in a 779-827 KB chunk, and is loaded by 816 of 830 routes (98%); dp-eval.mjs shows it evaluated on the first request of the storefront home and of /api/visit. /api/health loads 1.1 MB of JS and 779 KB of it is this chunk. Timed in this sandbox on an esbuild bundle of schema.ts: 105-134 ms to evaluate, 10-15 MB heap, then 31 ms and 5.8 MB for drizzle({schema}) against 0.04 ms without it.
findings.cost: About 136-165 ms and 16-21 MB of heap per cold start (sandbox figures, unbundled; an estimate for Vercel), and 600 KB of JS parsed, on 98% of routes including the health check and the page-view beacon.
findings.who_pays: The server on every cold start: the first shopper or owner after an idle spell, every cron wake of a cold function, and the deploy's health wait.
findings.fix: Three lines in src/db/client.ts: delete the schema import, call drizzle({ client: pool }), type Database as NodePgDatabase. schema.ts stays as drizzle-kit's source (drizzle.config.ts) and for the two scripts and one scan test that read it. Do this now as its own step; the file split that step 3.14 pairs it with can follow later. Then pnpm db:check must write no migration.
findings.saving: Measured here: 136-165 ms and about 16-21 MB heap less per cold start, 600 KB less server JS on 816 routes; /api/health drops from 1.1 MB to about 0.35 MB of JS (estimate from chunk sizes).
findings.risk: Low. No run-time code uses db.query or the typed tables. The type of Db changes shape only in its unused parts; the type check will show any stray use.
findings.already_tracked: docs/audits/code-review-2026-11.md step 3.14 (FD5), Open. It names the fix but ties it to splitting the file (effort M) in phase 3; nothing is measured there.

findings.title: sharp's native library, a font parser and a bzip reader load on nearly every cold start
findings.evidence: Twelve server modules start with `import sharp from "sharp"`, and they sit on static import chains from almost everything: the storefront layout reaches it through seo.ts, theme-store.ts, theme-shots.ts and theme-highlights.ts; the cart and the Stripe webhook through customers.ts, privacy-erasure.ts, data-jobs.ts and product-import.ts. In the build, sharp and libvips (18.9 MB) are in the file trace of 741 of 830 routes, and dp-eval.mjs finds the sharp external reached by eager imports from the entries of /api/visit (8 steps), the storefront home (7), checkout (7), the Stripe webhook (8) and the admin orders page (6). The same walk shows opentype.js (226 KB, used only to draw a brand mark for the AI manager) and seek-bzip (used only for Norwegian law archives) evaluated on the storefront home and the beacon; both are in 89% of routes. require('sharp') here: 37-56 ms and 22 MB RSS; opentype.js 11-12 ms and 2.2 MB heap.
findings.cost: About 50-70 ms and 24 MB of memory per cold start (sandbox figures) on 89% of routes for requests that never touch a picture or a font, plus 18.9 MB of native files in each of 741 routes' traces.
findings.who_pays: The server per cold start: shoppers' first page and beacon after idle, webhooks, owners' first admin page.
findings.fix: Load each at its call site: one helper (for example src/server/sharp-load.ts with `export const loadSharp = async () => (await import("sharp")).default`), `import type` for the types, and `await loadSharp()` inside the 12 modules' functions (sharp's own API is already async). The same one-line change in font-outlines.ts (`await import("opentype.js")` inside fontOutlines) and legal-sources.ts. Add a scan test that fails on a static value import of sharp, opentype.js or seek-bzip in src/server, beside the existing scan tests.
findings.saving: Estimate from the sandbox timings: 50-70 ms and about 24 MB RSS per cold start on roughly 740 routes. The trace still lists sharp until the import hub itself is cut; the load cost goes at once.
findings.risk: Low. The first picture job in an instance pays the 40-60 ms instead of every instance. Tests that mock sharp need the mock to cover the dynamic import.

findings.title: The Stripe and Supabase SDKs are evaluated by 97% of routes; reading a store builds a Stripe client to see if keys exist
findings.evidence: getStore() computes paymentsOn with platformModes() (stores.ts:300), which calls platformStripe(mode) and so constructs a Stripe client just to learn whether two environment keys are set (stripe.ts:58-60). stores.ts therefore imports stripe.ts, whose first line imports the SDK. Chain for the storefront: layout.tsx, fonts.ts, stores.ts, stripe.ts. In the build the Stripe SDK module (212 KB) is in the chunks of 804 of 830 routes and supabase-js (206 KB, reached from page.tsx through catalog.ts, custom-fields.ts, media.ts) in 803; dp-eval.mjs shows both evaluated on the first request of the storefront home and of /api/visit. Unbundled require here: stripe 47-69 ms and 4.3 MB heap, supabase-js 25-37 ms and 2.8 MB. 43 files import stripe.ts; clients are built at 67 call sites.
findings.cost: About 70-105 ms per cold start (sandbox figures, an estimate for Vercel) and 418 KB of JS on 97% of routes, most of which never call Stripe or Supabase storage.
findings.who_pays: The server per cold start; felt by the first shopper after idle and by the page-view beacon.
findings.fix: Step 1 (S): move platformModes() to a key-presence check in src/lib/stripe-account.ts (which already holds platformKey) so stores.ts no longer imports stripe.ts. Step 2 (M): make stripeFor() and platformStripe() async with `await import("stripe")` inside, keep `import type Stripe` elsewhere (21 files already do), and replace the six `instanceof Stripe.errors.StripeError` uses with one helper. Do the same for the storage client in media.ts and supabase-admin.ts. Measure a cold start before and after step 1 to decide how far to take step 2.
findings.saving: Estimate: 47-69 ms (Stripe) and 25-37 ms (supabase-js) per cold start on routes that do not use them. Step 1 alone saves nothing while other chains still reach stripe.ts; it removes the one chain that is there by accident.
findings.risk: Medium for step 2: 67 call sites gain an await, and webhook verification builds a client per request (api/stripe/webhook/[storeId]/route.ts:29). Covered by the payment integration suites.

findings.title: supabase-js and zod are 29% of the first scripts of every admin page
findings.evidence: The prerendered admin shell (.next/server/app/admin.html) has 15 scripts, 1,011 KB raw and 300 KB gzip. Two are libraries: the supabase-js chunk (179,419 bytes, 44,467 gzip) and the zod chunk (116,870, 32,733); both are named by all 432 admin route manifests and by no storefront one. supabase-js is there because SessionKeeper, drawn by the gated layout, statically imports the browser client to keep the token fresh; that client is the whole SDK (PostgREST, storage, realtime, functions). zod reaches the shell by three chains only: session.tsx to supabase/client.ts to env.ts (two strings checked), push-settings.tsx to lib/push.ts, and shortcut-sheet.tsx to responsive-edit.tsx to responsive.ts to typography.ts. dp-shell.mjs finds no other path to zod from the client components of the admin home, orders, products, customers, analytics or settings pages.
findings.cost: 296 KB raw / 77 KB gzip of script downloaded, parsed and run before the admin is usable, on every admin page; the admin's p75 largest paint is 3.93 s (psi-followups PERF-01).
findings.who_pays: An owner's browser on every admin page load.
findings.fix: (1) In session.tsx load the client inside the effects: `const { createClient } = await import("@/lib/supabase/client")`. (2) Give publicEnv() a zod-free home (two plain checks) so the browser client does not pull env.ts's zod. (3) Move the schemas of lib/push.ts and lib/typography.ts into push-schema.ts and typography-schema.ts, the convention docs/performance.md:34 already sets for visitors. (4) Extend storefront-bundle.scan.test.ts with a second entry set, the admin layouts' client components, so zod cannot come back into the shell. Lower the budgets in e2e/signed-in/admin-scripts.spec.ts:36 after.
findings.saving: 117 KB raw / 33 KB gzip gone from the first scripts of admin pages whose own forms do not use zod (home, orders, products, customers, analytics, settings: checked); 179 KB raw / 44 KB gzip moved off the critical path to after first paint. Together 29% of the shell's first scripts.
findings.risk: Low. The session keeper starts a moment later; its try/catch already tolerates failure. Pages with zod-based forms (builder, product editor) still load zod.
findings.already_tracked: Partly: docs/audits/psi-followups.md PERF-01 (open) sets the goal of cutting the admin's shared scripts; it does not name these two libraries. The visitor-side rule exists (performance.md:34) and stops at the admin.

findings.title: The rich text editor loads on 21 admin lists and detail pages that may never show it
findings.evidence: The tiptap/ProseMirror chunk is 435,421 bytes raw, 136,315 gzip, and 73 admin route manifests name it. 21 of them are not editors: the lists of pages, articles, headers, footers, product layouts and content, the category screens, and the order, customer and deal detail pages. Two static imports cause it: terms.tsx to term-page-fields.tsx to RichTextEditor (a category's description) and fields-form.tsx to RichTextEditor (a rich-text custom field; field_values has never held a row in production). The CSS editor in the same folder is already loaded with next/dynamic (css-panel.tsx:22). The budget file shows the price: the pages list's first scripts are 2.09 MB against 1.28 MB for the admin home.
findings.cost: 435 KB raw / 136 KB gzip of script on 21 screens whether or not an editor is drawn.
findings.who_pays: An owner's browser on the page, article and content lists and on every order, customer and deal page.
findings.fix: Wrap RichTextEditor in next/dynamic (ssr: false, a plain textarea-sized placeholder) where term-page-fields.tsx and fields-form.tsx use it, as css-panel.tsx does for CodeMirror. Then lower the /pages budget in admin-scripts.spec.ts and add /orders/{order} to it.
findings.saving: 435 KB raw / 136 KB gzip off the first scripts of 21 routes (measured chunk size; the exact drop per page to be read from the budget test).
findings.risk: Low. The editor appears a moment after the form; the builder's own pages are untouched.
findings.already_tracked: Adjacent: code review step 3.4 (FB8), Open, loads the builder's dialogs on demand; it does not cover these lists and detail pages.

findings.title: Nothing limits what a route's server function loads, so every route came to load everything
findings.evidence: The browser side has three guards (a static import scan for visitors, byte budgets for visitor routes, byte budgets for seven admin screens) and they have worked: shoppers' scripts are clean. The server side has none. Result, read from the build: the median route loads 11.6 MB of server JS; /api/visit evaluates 1,415 of 1,456 modules and its trace is 47.5 MB; /api/health's trace is 15.6 MB, 12.7 MB of it product-taxonomy data that one `/**` line (next.config.ts:69) adds to all 830 routes. There is also no unused-dependency check in CI (only pnpm audit). docs/performance.md, capacity.md and build-memory.md say nothing about cold start or trace size.
findings.cost: No direct cost; it is why DP-1, DP-2 and DP-3 could grow unnoticed, and each new feature added to a hub module now lands in every function.
findings.who_pays: Every later change; CI would carry the check (seconds, it reads files the build already wrote).
findings.fix: Two checks. (1) A scan test like storefront-bundle.scan.test.ts for server entries: the storefront layout and page, /api/visit, /api/speed, /api/health and the Stripe webhook may not statically reach sharp, opentype.js, playwright-core, owner-tools.ts or dream-factory.ts. (2) A post-build script in CI's build job that reads each listed route's page.js or route.js chunk list and .nft.json and fails over a byte budget (start at today's figure plus 4%, as the admin budgets do) or on a new external. The scratch scripts dp-route-libs.mjs, dp-eval.mjs and dp-nft.mjs under /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-kaizen-store/875cb21b-0ebd-5663-b7c0-2d04a7548e24/scratchpad/work are working prototypes. Optionally add knip to the static job for unused dependencies and exports.
findings.saving: Holds the gains of DP-1 to DP-3 and makes the import hub's size a number that can only fall. Estimate: none by itself.
findings.risk: Low. Budgets need raising on purpose now and then; that is the point.
findings.already_tracked: no (code review step 4.1, lint rules for the boundaries, is the nearest and is Open; it does not measure what a route loads)

findings.title: Three 125 MB Chromium functions are woken every minute and almost always find nothing
findings.evidence: /api/cron/cookie-scan, /api/cron/page-looks and /api/cron/theme-shots each trace 125.6 MB (Chromium 66.8, playwright-core 11.1, sharp 18.9, taxonomy 12.7, chunks 14.0; sizes of the files in their .nft.json). pg_cron calls each every minute. Production's cron_jobs rows give their last runs as 0 ms, 0 ms and 26 ms, and the statistics file says they find nothing to do almost every time. Chromium itself is only started when there is work (browser.ts uses import()), which is well done; the wake-ups are the waste.
findings.cost: 4,320 function calls a day to the heaviest functions in the deployment, each also evaluating the 11 MB hub when cold (after every deploy).
findings.who_pays: The server (Vercel invocations) and the database (a net.http_post and a cron_jobs upsert per call).
findings.fix: Let the scheduler ask the database first: schedule one SQL statement that calls the route only when its queue has a due row (`select net.http_post(...) where exists (select from commerce.cookie_scans where status = 'queued' ...)`, likewise for theme_shots and page looks), or have the five-minute dispatcher start them when it sees work. Belongs with the scheduling review; listed here because the dependency is what makes these functions heavy.
findings.saving: Estimate: nearly all of 4,320 calls a day, since the three routes report no work on almost every run.
findings.risk: Low to medium: a queued job starts up to one scheduler tick later; the queue conditions must match what each runner picks up.

findings.title: A 26 MB icon package is installed and parsed each build for 26 paths
findings.evidence: brand-icon.tsx imports 26 named icons from simple-icons, which holds 3,467. The 26 paths total 19,982 bytes. The package is 26 MB installed and its entry module, which the bundler must read on every build to pick those 26, is 5.25 MB; the Vercel build runs without a cache and near its memory limit (docs/build-memory.md). LinkedIn's mark is already hand-kept in the same file (line 34-36) because the package dropped it. Tree-shaking does work: no unused icon is in any chunk.
findings.cost: 26 MB of install, a 5.25 MB module parsed per build, and a caret-ranged dependency that removes brands in major versions.
findings.who_pays: The build and CI installs; nobody at run time.
findings.fix: Copy the 26 paths and hex colours into a small data file beside brand-icon.tsx (as LinkedIn's already is) and remove simple-icons from package.json. The licence is CC0.
findings.saving: 26 MB less to install; one 5.25 MB parse less per build (the time and memory saved are small and not measured).
findings.risk: Low. A brand that redraws its mark must be updated by hand.

findings.title: The existing plan's dependency item (FH12) names the wrong package twice
findings.evidence: FH12 and step 4.4 (Open) say `three` is a dependency nothing imports and that `pg` should leave production dependencies. Both are wrong. `pg` is the production driver (client.ts:7, with the reason at :56-63); the driver with no run-time use is `postgres`, imported only by the build's host read (store-hosts-build.ts:1), five scripts, and tests, and found in no server chunk. `three` has no import in src because @google/model-viewer imports it as a required peer (wave-6-catalogue.md:838 says so); removing it breaks the 3D viewer. One real issue hides here: the peer range is ^0.183.0 and 0.187.0 is installed, which is outside it for a 0.x version.
findings.cost: No run-time cost. A plan step that, followed as written, removes the database driver from the list or breaks the 3D viewer.
findings.who_pays: Whoever picks up step 4.4; an agent's session reading the plan.
findings.fix: Correct FH12 and step 4.4 in the same change that touches them (the plan's own rule): `pg` stays; `postgres` may move to devDependencies only if the Vercel build keeps installing them (next.config.ts needs it at build time), otherwise leave it and say why; `three` stays as a peer, pinned to a version inside model-viewer's range (0.183.x) or with a note that 0.187 was tested with View in 3D.
findings.saving: None in bytes. Removes a wrong instruction from the working plan.
findings.risk: None for the doc fix. Changing three's version needs one look at a 3D product page.
findings.already_tracked: docs/audits/code-review-2026-11.md step 4.4 (FH12), Open, but incorrect as written
